SECTIONS {"slug":"thai-massage","width":390,"sections":[{"anchor":"ts-what-it-is","label":"What it is","text":"What Is Thai Massage?Thai massage brings movement and massage together through rhythmic compression, gentle rocking, and assisted stretching. It is my specialty. I set the pace and range of each movement by what is comfortable for you, so you have time to slow down while stiff areas get careful attention.As the session goes on, I apply steady pressure and guide you through stretches that can help you notice where your body feels restricted. Tell me what feels good, ask for a lighter touch, or skip a movement at any point. I want you to feel supported the whole way through.Thai massage suits people who enjoy hands-on bodywork but also want gentle movement. You stay fully clothed, so wear something loose and comfortable. I shape each session around the person in front of me, so the work can be restful, more active, or a blend of both.Traditional Thai massage traces its roots to everyday self-care in Thai villages, and in 2019 UNESCO added Nuad Thai, traditional Thai massage, to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.[1] I trained in traditional Thai bodywork at Still Light Center."},{"anchor":"ts-common-reasons","label":"Common reasons","text":"Common Reasons Clients Choose Thai MassagePeople often come to Thai massage when long hours at a desk, travel, exercise, or everyday routines leave them stiff and wanting to move more freely. Others simply like the combination of steady pressure, gentle rocking, and assisted stretching as a way to unwind.I begin with your goals and comfort level. If your shoulders, hips, or back feel tight, I can spend more time there and still give the rest of your body its share. I guide stretches and never force them, and you can ask me to change or leave out any movement.Whether this is your first Thai massage or you have had many, tell me about any health concerns or movement limits before the session begins. Then you and I can decide what feels right that day."},{"anchor":"ts-what-to-expect","label":"What to expect","text":"What To Expect During Your Appointment Before your session, tell me about any health conditions, medications, pregnancy, recent injury or surgery. I may adjust the work, or suggest you check with your clinician first. New numbness, weakness, unexplained swelling or radiating pain means you should see a doctor before massage. Consultation and AssessmentI start with a short conversation about how you are feeling, which areas feel stiff, and how much movement and pressure you would enjoy. Personalized Session PlanYou choose a comfortable pace, and I adjust the mix of rhythmic pressure, gentle rocking, and assisted stretches to your goals for the session. Thai Massage SessionI guide each movement and check in as I go. You can ask for less pressure, a smaller stretch, or a different approach at any time. Post-Session GuidanceBefore you leave, I can suggest a few simple ways to hold on to that sense of ease, based on how your body responded."},{"anchor":"ts-guide-questions","label":"Questions","text":"Questions About Thai Massage What Should I Wear to a Thai Massage?You stay fully clothed, so wear something loose and comfortable that lets you move easily. What Will I Lie On?Thai massage is done on a mat. I guide each movement and check in with you as I go. How Long Is a Session?Sessions are 60 or 90 minutes. If you are not sure which to choose, tell me what you would like from the session and I will help you decide. Do I Need to Be Flexible?No. I set the range of each stretch by what is comfortable for you, and I never force one. You can ask me to change or skip any movement. Where Do Sessions Take Place?Right now I offer corporate and group massage only, at suitable Portland venues, with bookings beginning November 14, 2026. Individual appointments at a dedicated Thai Solitude location are planned for summer 2027. I do not offer individual home visits. How Is Thai Massage Different From Your Other Services?Thai massage is done fully clothed on a mat and combines steady pressure and gentle rocking with assisted stretching. Therapeutic Massage and Deep Tissue Massage are described on their own pages. How Do I Book a Session?Corporate and group massage bookings begin November 14, 2026. The Corporate & Group Massage page explains how to request a quote. Individual appointments are planned for summer 2027. Other services: Therapeutic massage · Deep tissue massage · Chair massage · Corporate & group massage"},{"anchor":"ts-guide-research","label":"What Research Says","text":"What the Research Says About Thai Massage Research on traditional Thai massage is still limited. Most studies are small, many compare Thai massage with another approach rather than with no massage, and most follow people for only a few weeks. The summaries below describe what the studies reported. They are general information, not medical advice or a promise of any result, and people respond differently. This section covers studies of massage for pain, movement, stress, energy and recovery; studies of massage used for specific medical conditions are not summarized here. Each part starts with what the studies found in massage’s favor, then gives the results that were weaker, mixed or negative, and ends on what is encouraging: I included the studies I found with disappointing results, not only the favorable ones. Reviews, and What They Say About Limits A 2015 systematic review of six studies of traditional Thai massage in people with long-lasting pain found that every study reported less pain after a course of sessions, with the reduction appearing to last for up to 15 weeks.[2] A 2012 review of six studies of Swedish and Thai massage for low-back pain reported that the two appeared to be about equally helpful.[3] The reviews also say what they could not show. The 2015 review’s authors said more research is needed to learn how Thai massage compares with control conditions over the longer term, and the 2012 review noted that weaknesses in the studies mean more direct comparisons are needed. Reviews of massage in general are cautious, too. A 2015 Cochrane review of 25 trials with 3,096 people with low-back pain found some short-term benefits, but the studies were small and of low quality, and its authors said they had “very little confidence” in the results.[4] A 2024 Cochrane review of 33 studies with 1,994 people with neck pain found that massage probably made little or no difference compared with a placebo massage after about 12 weeks (low-certainty evidence).[5] That neck review also found that higher doses, meaning eight or more sessions of at least 30 minutes over four weeks, favored massage in a subgroup analysis, which suggests that regular sessions may matter.[5] Massage is generally described as low risk, and where serious problems on record can be traced to who gave the massage, they are mostly tied to people who were not trained massage therapists. The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health notes that the risk of harm appears to be low, although rare serious side effects such as a blood clot, nerve injury or bone fracture have been reported.[6] A 2014 review of 40 published reports found 138 adverse events over 11 years, mainly disc herniation, soft-tissue injury, nerve problems, spinal cord injury and tears in the neck arteries, with spinal manipulation inside a massage repeatedly linked to the serious ones. Massage therapists were the practitioners in only 8 of the 138 events (5.8 percent) and chiropractors in 33 (23.9 percent); the rest (70.3 percent) involved unregistered people or other health professionals, and the authors concluded that massage by nonprofessionals and forceful techniques is often associated with adverse events.[7] A 2003 review of 16 case reports and four case series likewise found that most adverse effects followed exotic techniques or massage by laypeople, with massage therapists rarely implicated, that serious effects were mostly tied to techniques other than Swedish massage, and concluded that serious events are probably true rarities.[8] For Thai massage specifically, a 2019 case report described a 20-year-old man who developed bleeding around the spinal cord (a spinal epidural hematoma) with delayed leg weakness three days after a Thai massage given by a layperson, a friend, and who needed emergency surgery.[9] A 2015 commentary also discussed a patient who had a heart attack around the time of a Thai massage and the possible adverse effects of Thai massage.[10] The U.S. center also advises against using massage to put off seeing a health care provider about a medical problem. Taken together, in the reports that say who gave the massage, trained massage therapists were rarely involved: the serious injuries were mostly linked to people who were not massage therapists, including laypeople and unregistered practitioners, and to forceful or unusual techniques. Serious events are rare: I ask about your health, medications and recent injuries before each session, and I set the pressure and the range of each stretch by what is comfortable for you. Back Pain Two trials with a comparison that was not another massage reported clear differences. In 50 adults with upper-back pain, one 30-minute session of Thai massage was followed by larger reductions in pain, muscle tension and muscle activity than a sham device.[11] In 36 adults with back pain, one 30-minute session was followed by lower self-reported pain, anxiety and muscle tension and better flexibility than resting on a bed.[12] Trials that compared Thai massage with another approach found similar results rather than a winner. In a hospital trial in Bangkok, 120 adults had Thai massage or joint mobilization twice a week for four weeks, and both groups improved by similar amounts on pain and everyday-activity scores. The trial had no comparison group that received neither, so it cannot show how much of the change was due to the sessions themselves.[13] In 140 older adults, Thai massage alone and Thai massage with an herbal compress led to similar improvements over 15 weeks, so the compress added no clear benefit.[14] In another trial of 140 adults, adding acupuncture to court-type Thai massage made no clear difference after one month, and both groups reported less pain and more movement.[15] A preliminary trial of 18 military personnel with back pain found less pain after both Thai massage and acupuncture, with one pain-questionnaire score lower after acupuncture.[16] An earlier trial that compared Thai and Swedish massage for back pain with tender spots in the muscles found that pain fell by more than half in both groups after three weeks and stayed lower for up to a month, with no significant difference between them.[17] Neck, Shoulders, Arms and Feet In 45 adults with neck pain, eight sessions of Thai massage or of a muscle energy technique over two weeks were each followed by more improvement in pain and neck movement than in a control group.[18] In 78 adults with shoulder-blade pain, four weeks of Thai massage or Thai boxing exercise both reduced pain, and Thai massage did better on several measures, including pain and neck movement, at the end of the program and at one month.[19] In 46 adults with upper-shoulder pain, court-type Thai massage and a Thai hermit exercise routine both improved neck movement and pain, and the massage group reported a clearer reduction in pain.[20] In 62 young adults with tender spots in the forearm muscles, nine short sessions of Thai massage were followed by greater improvement in pain, tenderness and wrist movement than sham ultrasound.[21] Not every comparison favored Thai massage. In the neck trial there was no clear difference between Thai massage and the muscle energy technique. In 60 people with heel pain, both Thai massage and ultrasound were followed by less pain, but ultrasound with stretching produced larger gains in pain and ankle movement.[22] In 48 adults with a forward head posture, a four-week program that combined Thai massage with shoulder-blade exercises and chest mobilization improved head position and neck movement more than lying at rest. Because three approaches were combined, the trial cannot show what Thai massage added by itself.[23] In 30 healthy female office workers who each tried three styles of Thai massage, the authors reported that “strength in shoulders was not significantly different, but some forearm fatigue was decreased significantly among the three massage techniques.”[24] A pilot trial of 20 people with shoulder-blade pain found lower pain and muscle tension after Thai massage than after a physical-therapy package of ultrasound and a hot pack.[25] Stress, Energy and Recovery In 54 healthy adults whose calf muscles were tired by heel-raise exercise, 30 minutes of Thai massage was followed by faster recovery on muscle measures than 30 minutes of mostly rest.[26] In 34 soccer players who were given Thai massage or rest, all seven fitness tests (sit-and-reach, hand grip strength, agility, a 50-meter sprint, sit-ups, push-ups and a test of aerobic fitness) improved in the massage group, compared with two in the rest group.[27] The results on stress are mixed. Two small trials in healthy adults first raised stress with a mental-arithmetic test and then gave either one hour of Thai massage or one hour of rest. In both trials, stress measures fell after massage and after rest. In one trial (29 people, each trying both), one marker, salivary amylase, fell more after Thai massage; in the other (30 people), no measure differed between the groups.[28][29] In 36 physiotherapy students under academic stress, saliva cortisol and heart rate fell after one Thai massage session and in a control group, with no significant difference in cortisol between the groups.[30] In a small crossover trial, 20 adults who felt tired or low on energy had three weekly sessions of Thai massage and three of Swedish massage, and Swedish massage was described as having the larger effect on relaxation and sleep.[31] Even so, the results point the same encouraging way on the outcomes that matter to many people: a marker of stress, salivary amylase, fell more after Thai massage than after rest in one trial,[28] and in the trial of tired adults Thai massage was described as the more energizing of the two styles.[31] Sources Each number above links to the source. Two small trials in healthy adults first raised stress with a mental-arithmetic test and then gave either one hour of Thai massage or one hour of rest. In both trials, stress measures fell after massage and after rest. In one trial (29 people, each trying both), one marker, salivary amylase, fell more after Thai massage; in the other (30 people), no measure differed between the groups.[28][29] In 36 physiotherapy students under academic stress, saliva cortisol and heart rate fell after one Thai massage session and in a control group, with no significant difference in cortisol between the groups.[30] In a small crossover trial, 20 adults who felt tired or low on energy had three weekly sessions of Thai massage and three of Swedish massage, and Swedish massage was described as having the larger effect on relaxation and sleep.[31] Even so, the results point the same encouraging way on the outcomes that matter to many people: a marker of stress, salivary amylase, fell more after Thai massage than after rest in one trial,[28] and in the trial of tired adults Thai massage was described as the more energizing of the two styles.[31] Sources Each number above links to the source. SECTIONS {"slug":"therapeutic-massage","width":390,"sections":[{"anchor":"ts-what-it-is","label":"What it is","text":"What Is Therapeutic Massage?Therapeutic massage combines focused work with time to relax. I start with what brought you in. You can ask me to stay with one area, such as your neck and shoulders, or to work more broadly, and the plan can change as you give me feedback.Research suggests that massage therapy may help reduce pain in some conditions and may improve certain movement-related outcomes in studied pain populations.[1][2] Studies of sports massage have found small improvements in flexibility and exercise-related muscle soreness.[3] Brief massage has been studied for short-term relaxation.[4] Regular massage was associated with improved well-being in a small four-week study of older adults.[5]Some studies have looked at massage in family caregivers.[6] Research has also examined massage in relation to stress and quality-of-life measures in specific adult groups.[7][8][5] These are general findings, not medical advice or a promise of any result; the full summaries, including the weaker results, are in the research section below."},{"anchor":"ts-common-reasons","label":"Common reasons","text":"Common Reasons Clients Choose Therapeutic MassagePeople often book therapeutic massage for everyday muscle tension and stiffness, or simply to make time to slow down. Some also seek focused work for neck or shoulder discomfort, and I adapt the pace and pressure to what suits you. Research on massage for neck and shoulder pain is mixed. It may help some people for a short time,[9] but a 2024 Cochrane review found that, for neck pain, massage probably makes little or no difference compared with a placebo massage.[10] A subgroup analysis in that review favored higher doses (eight or more sessions of at least 30 minutes over four weeks), which suggests that regular sessions may matter.[10] Massage has also been studied for low-back pain, although the evidence is limited.[9] Before I begin, I ask about your preferences and anything I should know about your health. You can request lighter pressure, a different focus, or a pause at any time."},{"anchor":"ts-who-can-benefit","label":"Who can benefit","text":"Who Can Benefit From Therapeutic Massage?Therapeutic massage can be adapted to many goals, from a calm session to focused work on areas of tension. If you have an ongoing health condition or a new symptom, tell me at the start. I will keep the work within the scope of massage, and I will tell you if I think you should check with a doctor first."},{"anchor":"ts-guide-questions","label":"Questions","text":"Questions About Therapeutic Massage What Is the Difference Between Therapeutic and Relaxation Massage?Relaxation massage prioritizes a calm experience. Therapeutic massage can give more attention to a particular area of tension while still adapting pressure and pace to your comfort. It does not have to mean intense or painful pressure. How Is a Therapeutic Session Planned?Start by telling me what you would like from the session. Before I begin, I talk through the areas of focus, pace, and pressure with you. Will I Feel the Results Right Away?People respond differently to massage, so I can’t promise a particular result or timeline. I will ask how the session feels and adjust as I go. How Often Should I Come In for Therapeutic Massage?There is no schedule that suits everyone. You decide whether another session makes sense, and I am glad to talk through your goals with you first. Is Therapeutic Massage Appropriate If I Have No Specific Complaint?Yes. You don’t need a particular area of concern to book. You can come simply to make time for yourself, slow down, and receive attentive care without arriving with a specific complaint or goal. Tell me what kind of session would feel good, and I’ll plan around that. Can I Ask You to Focus on My Neck and Shoulders?Yes. Tell me at the start where you would like the focus, and you can change it at any point during the session. For anything new, severe, or worrying, please see a doctor first. How Is Therapeutic Massage Different From Deep Tissue Massage?Therapeutic massage gives steady attention to the places where you feel tension, at a pace and pressure that suit you. Deep tissue massage uses focused strokes and sustained pressure on areas that stay tight. I check in about pressure in both, and each is described on its own page. Can I Change the Pressure During a Session?Yes. You can ask for lighter pressure, a different focus, or a pause at any time, and I will adjust. Where Do Sessions Take Place?Right now I offer corporate and group massage only, at suitable Portland venues, with bookings beginning November 14, 2026. Individual appointments at a dedicated Thai Solitude location are planned for summer 2027. I do not offer individual home visits. How Do I Book a Session?Corporate and group massage bookings begin November 14, 2026. The Corporate & Group Massage page explains how to request a quote. Individual appointments are planned for summer 2027."},{"anchor":"ts-what-to-expect","label":"What to expect","text":"What To Expect During Your Appointment Before your session, tell me about any health conditions, medications, pregnancy, recent injury or surgery. I may adjust the work, or suggest you check with your clinician first. New numbness, weakness, unexplained swelling or radiating pain means you should see a doctor before massage. Consultation and AssessmentI begin with a short conversation about where you’re holding tension, what’s been bothering you, and how you would like to feel when the session ends. Planning the SessionFrom there, I plan the session around your goals: full-body relaxation, focused work on one area, or some of each. Therapeutic Massage WorkI work from surface tension toward deeper tightness, adjusting pressure and pace as the session goes on. Post-Session GuidanceAt the end, I ask how the work felt and answer any questions about future sessions. Other services: Thai massage · Deep tissue massage · Chair massage · Corporate & group massage"},{"anchor":"ts-guide-research","label":"What Research Says","text":"What the Research Says About Therapeutic Massage Research on massage therapy is large but mixed. Many studies are small, results often depend on what massage is compared with, and many follow people for only a few weeks. The summaries below describe what the studies reported. They are general information, not medical advice or a promise of any result, and people respond differently. This section covers studies of massage for pain, movement, soreness, stress and well-being; studies of massage used for specific medical conditions are not summarized here. Each part starts with what the studies found in massage’s favor, then gives the results that were weaker, mixed or negative, and ends on what is encouraging: I included the studies I found with disappointing results, not only the favorable ones. Reviews, and What They Say About Limits Reviews that rated how certain their evidence was reached a consistent point in massage’s favor: every conclusion rated moderate-certainty found massage associated with less pain, and a meta-analysis of 67 randomized trials found lower pain scores after massage than after sham massage, no massage or other approaches.[1][2] The same reviews are careful about limits. None of the conclusions in the 2024 review was rated high-certainty, and conclusions backed by moderate- or high-certainty evidence that massage was better than other active approaches were rare. An earlier evidence map of 49 systematic reviews found that the high-quality reviews reached conclusions of low strength of evidence, because few large, rigorous studies had been done.[11] The meta-analysis’s authors made a strong recommendation only for the comparison with no massage and a weak one for sham massage and other approaches.[2] A 2015 review of 26 randomized trials with 2,565 people with muscle and joint problems found low-to-moderate-level evidence that massage reduced pain in the short term compared with no intervention in some groups, such as people with shoulder pain, but not in people with neck or low-back pain. Function improved in the short term for people with low-back and shoulder pain. Compared with another active approach, no clear benefit was seen.[12] Massage is generally described as low risk, and where serious problems on record can be traced to who gave the massage, they are mostly tied to people who were not trained massage therapists. The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health notes that the risk of harm appears to be low, although rare serious side effects such as a blood clot, nerve injury or bone fracture have been reported.[9] A 2014 review of 40 published reports found 138 adverse events over 11 years, mainly disc herniation, soft-tissue injury, nerve problems, spinal cord injury and tears in the neck arteries, with spinal manipulation inside a massage repeatedly linked to the serious ones. Massage therapists were the practitioners in only 8 of the 138 events (5.8 percent) and chiropractors in 33 (23.9 percent); the rest (70.3 percent) involved unregistered people or other health professionals, and the authors concluded that massage by nonprofessionals and forceful techniques is often associated with adverse events.[13] A 2003 review of 16 case reports and four case series likewise found that most adverse effects followed exotic techniques or massage by laypeople, with massage therapists rarely implicated, that serious effects were mostly tied to techniques other than Swedish massage, and concluded that serious events are probably true rarities.[14] The U.S. center also advises against using massage to put off seeing a health care provider about a medical problem. Taken together, in the reports that say who gave the massage, trained massage therapists were rarely involved: the serious injuries were mostly linked to people who were not massage therapists, including laypeople and unregistered practitioners, and to forceful or unusual techniques. Serious events are rare: I ask about your health, medications, pregnancy and recent injuries before each session, and you can ask for lighter pressure or a pause at any time. Neck, Shoulders and Back Several reviews report short-term gains from massage for neck, shoulder and back pain. A 2015 Cochrane review of 25 trials found that massage was better than no intervention for low-back pain in the short term.[15] A 2014 review of 20 trials found low-quality evidence that soft-tissue massage improved shoulder movement, pain and function compared with no intervention in the short term, right after the sessions ended.[16] In the 2024 Cochrane review of neck pain, a subgroup analysis favored higher doses of eight or more sessions of at least 30 minutes over four weeks.[10] The same reviews also report the limits. The low-back review rated the quality of the evidence low to very low, found no long-term benefit over no intervention, and its authors said they had “very little confidence” in the results. No serious side effects were reported; the most common minor one was more pain, in 1.5 to 25 percent of people.[15] The 2024 neck review of 33 studies with 1,994 people found that, compared with a placebo massage, massage probably makes little or no difference to pain, function or quality of life at up to 12 weeks (low-certainty evidence), and adverse events were too poorly reported to judge.[10] In a trial of 80 adults with shoulder pain who were all doing exercises, adding four weeks of massage gave no extra benefit for pain, disability or movement, and a small difference in pain at 12 weeks favored exercise alone.[17] In 41 people with low-back pain who were all having physiotherapy, adding real massage or a placebo massage for three weeks both reduced pain and disability and improved mobility, and only the real-massage group improved on a quality-of-life measure.[18] Smaller studies point the same encouraging way for tight shoulder muscles. In a crossover study of 17 healthy adults, muscle activity in the upper-shoulder muscles fell by 19 percent after a short, moderate-pressure massage of the shoulders and neck, compared with 1 percent after sitting quietly; the study measured muscle activity, not pain.[19] In a pilot study of 45 cardiac sonographers with work-related muscle discomfort, weekly 30-minute chair massages for 10 weeks, with or without stretching, were followed by some improvement in discomfort scores compared with no intervention, and the authors called for larger trials.[20] Exercise, Flexibility and Recovery Of the exercise outcomes reviewed, flexibility and soreness are where massage shows benefit. A 2020 review of 29 randomized studies with 1,012 people found small improvements in flexibility and in delayed-onset muscle soreness.[3] In 10 recreationally active women, 30 seconds of massage at the back of the thigh was followed by about a 7 percent larger hip-bend range than no massage, with no change in muscle tension or muscle activity.[21] In 52 healthy volunteers whose grip had been tired by exercise, five minutes of forearm and hand massage was followed by better grip performance than five minutes of rest or of passive joint movement; the study was small and measured only the minutes right afterward.[22] The same 2020 review found no evidence that massage improved strength, jumping, sprinting, endurance or fatigue.[3] A 2016 review of 22 trials concluded that the effects of massage on performance recovery are rather small and partly unclear, and its authors questioned whether the limited effects justify using massage as a recovery method in competitive athletes.[23] In 62 healthy active students who had a 40-minute whole-body myofascial-release massage after hard exercise, massage was followed by lower muscle activity in a thigh muscle and a lower mood score for vigor than a sham session, which the authors said may reflect a transient loss of muscle strength or a state of relaxation.[24] In people with sore leg muscles after exercise, manual massage, real diathermy (a heating device) and sham diathermy produced no clinically relevant differences in pain scores right after the session, although scores on a patient-rated scale of global change did differ between the groups.[25] Where massage has been tested for short-term recovery after intense mixed training, the effects were medium in size: the 2016 review found medium positive effects after high-intensity mixed exercise, and shorter massage (5 to 12 minutes) tended to show larger effects than longer massage.[23] Stress, Relaxation and Well-Being Several studies point to short-term relaxation after massage. A 2004 meta-analysis of 37 randomized studies found that a single massage was followed by lower state anxiety, blood pressure and heart rate.[26] In 60 healthy women, the two massage groups showed higher heart-rate variability than a resting group.[4] In 118 healthy adults who first took a stressful laboratory test, most people who had a real rhythmical massage described it as relaxing (82 to 100 percent, compared with 42 percent after a sham massage).[27] The picture is mixed, though. The same 2004 meta-analysis found no lower negative mood, cortisol or less immediate pain after a single massage,[26] and a 2011 review found that the effect on the stress hormone cortisol was generally very small and in most analyses not statistically distinguishable from zero.[28] In the 60 healthy women, relaxation rose and stress fell in the resting group too.[4] In the 118 healthy adults, a single rhythmical massage of about an hour was not followed by significantly better well-being scores or cortisol levels than a sham massage.[27] In 14 healthy men, a 20-minute massage and a 20-minute reading period were each followed by a rise in the hormone oxytocin, which led the researchers to suggest that touch is not needed for that rise.[29] In 15 healthy women, a single two-minute manual massage was not followed by significant differences in heart-rate variability or blood pressure compared with rest or a sham, although the authors noted changes of moderate to large size within the massage condition.[30] In 38 family caregivers at a rehabilitation hospital who had either one or three massages a week for two weeks, psychological symptom scores were lower afterward in both groups, but because everyone had massage the study cannot show how much of the change was due to the massage itself.[6] Courses of massage have the more encouraging results: the largest effects in the 2004 meta-analysis came after a course of sessions rather than a single one, on measures of anxiety and mood.[26] In a pilot study of 54 adults aged 60 and over, twice-weekly massage for four weeks was followed by better scores for well-being and perceived stress than guided relaxation.[5] In a trial of 122 adults at an integrative-therapy clinic in Brazil, people had eight Anma (Japanese) massage sessions followed by rest, massage followed by Reiki, or no intervention. Stress fell more in the massage-plus-Reiki group than in the no-intervention group, and the authors called for a placebo group in later trials.[7] The same trial’s report on stress and quality of life (101 people analyzed) found that both massage groups did better than no intervention.[8] Sources Each number above links to the source. SECTIONS {"slug":"deep-tissue-massage","width":390,"sections":[{"anchor":"ts-what-it-is","label":"What it is","text":"What Is Deep Tissue Massage?Deep tissue massage uses slow, deliberate pressure on muscles that stay tight. I begin by asking about your goals and how much pressure you like, then check in as I work. Deep pressure is never required: you can ask me to lighten up at any time, and I will.Research on deep tissue massage is limited and mixed. In a trial of 80 adults with neck pain linked to tender spots in the muscles, adding deep tissue massage to conventional rehabilitation was followed by more improvement in pain, quality-of-life scores and most neck movements than rehabilitation alone.[1] A larger trial of 619 adults with ongoing neck pain found that deep tissue massage led to more improvement in pain than advice to stay active in the short term but not by 12 months, and a review of the research found that studies differ too much in what they call deep tissue massage and how they do it to draw clear conclusions.[2][3] People given massage, exercise or both in that larger trial were also more likely than those given advice to say they had recovered, at every follow-up through one year.[2] These are general findings, not medical advice or a promise of any result; the full summaries, including the weaker results, are in the research section below."},{"anchor":"ts-common-reasons","label":"Common reasons","text":"Common Reasons Clients Choose Deep Tissue MassagePeople often choose deep tissue massage when an area stays tight after work, exercise, or daily routines. I focus on the areas you point out and adjust pressure as you tell me how it feels."},{"anchor":"ts-what-to-expect","label":"What to expect","text":"What To Expect During Your Appointment Before your session, tell me about any health conditions, medications, pregnancy, recent injury or surgery. I may adjust the work, or suggest you check with your clinician first. New numbness, weakness, unexplained swelling or radiating pain means you should see a doctor before massage. If you have severe pain, seek medical evaluation before booking massage. Consultation and AssessmentI begin by asking where you want me to focus, how much pressure you like, and anything about your health or past injuries I should know. Planning the SessionFrom your answers, I decide where to spend the most time and which techniques and pressure to use, and I tell you the plan before I start. Other services: Thai massage · Therapeutic massage · Chair massage · Corporate & group massage"},{"anchor":"ts-guide-research","label":"What Research Says","text":"What the Research Says About Deep Tissue Massage Research on deep tissue massage is limited, and the studies are hard to compare: a 2018 review found no commonly accepted definition of deep tissue massage, and the studies used different techniques and protocols.[3] Many studies are small, results often depend on what massage is compared with, and many follow people for only a few weeks. The summaries below describe what the studies reported. They are general information, not medical advice or a promise of any result, and people respond differently. This section covers studies of massage for pain, movement, soreness, recovery and relaxation; studies of massage used for specific medical conditions are not summarized here. Each part starts with what the studies found in massage’s favor, then gives the results that were weaker, mixed or negative, and ends on what is encouraging: I included the studies I found with disappointing results, not only the favorable ones. Reviews, and What They Say About Limits Reviews of massage in general, not only deep tissue massage, reached a consistent point in massage’s favor: every conclusion rated moderate-certainty found massage associated with less pain, and a meta-analysis of 67 randomized trials found lower pain scores after massage than after sham massage, no massage or other approaches.[4][5] A 2018 review of the research on deep tissue massage itself reported that favorable outcomes may result in people with pain and in people with decreased range of motion.[3] The same reviews are careful about limits. None of the conclusions in the 2024 review was rated high-certainty, and conclusions backed by moderate- or high-certainty evidence that massage was better than other active approaches were rare.[4] An earlier evidence map of 49 systematic reviews found that the high-quality reviews reached conclusions of low strength of evidence, because few large, rigorous studies had been done.[6] The meta-analysis’s authors made a strong recommendation only for the comparison with no massage and a weak one for sham massage and other approaches.[5] The 2018 review of deep tissue massage found that the techniques and protocols used in published studies differed so much that it was difficult to draw any clear conclusions, and its authors asked for future research to use a common definition and common comparison groups.[3] Massage is generally described as low risk, but deep pressure deserves a plain account of the rare serious events on record. The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health notes that the risk of harm appears to be low, although rare serious side effects such as a blood clot, nerve injury or bone fracture have been reported.[7] The 2018 review of deep tissue massage found several rare serious adverse events related to it, probably as a result of the forceful application of massage therapy.[3] Published case reports describe a blocked artery to part of a kidney in a healthy man about four hours after a deep tissue massage for low back pain given by an unlicensed therapist,[8] a blood clot in a neck vein after a deep tissue massage focused on the neck,[9] a blood clot in a vein after vigorous deep tissue massage in a previously healthy 67-year-old man, whose authors suggested that vigorous massage of the legs be considered a possible risk factor for such clots, especially in older adults,[10] and an injury to a nerve that left a shoulder muscle weak after deep tissue massage.[11] Single case reports show that something happened, not how often. A 2014 review of 40 published reports of massage found 138 adverse events over 11 years, mainly disc herniation, soft-tissue injury, nerve problems, spinal cord injury and tears in the neck arteries, with spinal manipulation inside a massage repeatedly linked to the serious ones. Massage therapists were the practitioners in only 8 of the 138 events (5.8 percent) and chiropractors in 33 (23.9 percent); the rest (70.3 percent) involved unregistered people or other health professionals, and the authors concluded that massage by nonprofessionals and forceful techniques is often associated with adverse events.[12] A 2003 review of 16 case reports and four case series likewise found that most adverse effects followed exotic techniques or massage by laypeople, with massage therapists rarely implicated, that serious effects were mostly tied to techniques other than Swedish massage, and concluded that serious events are probably true rarities.[13] The U.S. center also advises against using massage to put off seeing a health care provider about a medical problem. Taken together, serious events are rare and, where the reports say who gave the massage, they were mostly linked to people who were not massage therapists and to forceful or unusual techniques. Deep pressure is never required: before your session I ask you to tell me about health conditions, medications, pregnancy and recent injury or surgery, and you can ask for lighter pressure or a pause at any time. Neck, Shoulders and Back Several trials of deep tissue massage report short-term gains for neck and back pain. In 80 adults with neck pain linked to tender spots in the muscles, one group had 12 sessions of deep tissue massage on top of electrical stimulation, hot packs and ultrasound, and the other had only those three; the massage group improved more on pain, a neck-disability score and a quality-of-life score, and on neck extension, side bending and turning, but not on forward bending.[1] In 64 adults, 60 of whom finished, with chronic low back pain that had no specific cause, tender-point deep tissue massage plus lumbar traction was followed by a higher pressure pain threshold, less muscle hardness and less pain than traction alone: pain scores fell by 1.9 with massage and 1.4 with traction alone.[14] In 26 adults aged 60 to 75 with chronic low back pain, ten days of deep tissue massage and ten days of therapeutic massage both improved pain and disability scores, and deep tissue massage did better on one disability score and on pain.[15] In 40 office workers with chronic low back pain, four 45-minute deep tissue massage sessions over two weeks were followed by better lower-back movement and lower pain ratings in the massage group, while the group given no therapy showed no significant changes.[16] A 2015 Cochrane review of 25 trials found that massage was better than no intervention for low-back pain in the short term.[17] The larger and more carefully designed studies are more cautious. In the Stockholm Neck trial of 619 adults with ongoing neck pain, deep tissue massage led to a higher chance of improvement in pain than advice to stay active in the short term but not at later follow-ups, and at 12 months none of the therapies tested was more effective than advice for pain intensity or for pain-related disability.[2] A cost analysis of the same trial found that massage and the combined therapy cost more and were less beneficial than advice, that differences in health-related quality of life were minimal, and its authors concluded that massage and the combined therapy are not cost-effective.[18] The 2024 Cochrane review of massage for neck pain, which included 33 studies with 1,994 people, found that, compared with a placebo massage, massage probably makes little or no difference to pain, function or quality of life at up to 12 weeks (low-certainty evidence), and adverse events were too poorly reported to judge.[19] The 2015 Cochrane review of low-back pain rated the quality of the evidence low to very low, found no long-term benefit over no intervention, and its authors said they had “very little confidence” in the results.[17] In 59 adults with chronic low back pain who had two weeks of deep tissue massage with or without a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, pain and function improved in both groups with no difference between them; because everyone had massage, the trial cannot show how much of the change was due to the massage itself.[20] In the office-worker trial, the two groups differed significantly in only one lower-back movement, and the authors said larger studies and an assessment of long-term effects are needed.[16] The small trial of 26 older adults ended by saying that further research is needed.[15] Still, people in the Stockholm Neck trial who had massage, exercise or both were more likely than those given advice to say they had recovered, at every follow-up through one year.[2] A subgroup analysis in the 2024 Cochrane review favored higher doses (eight or more sessions of at least 30 minutes over four weeks), which suggests that regular sessions may matter.[19] Exercise, Soreness and Recovery Deep massage has shown benefit in a laboratory model of muscle soreness: in a double-blinded randomized trial in volunteers whose forearm muscles were made sore with exercise, deep tissue massage reduced pain during a muscle stretch (about a 48 percent reversal of the soreness), and both deep massage and light touch reduced sensitivity to pressure compared with a group that had no massage.[21] A 2020 review of 29 randomized studies with 1,012 people found small improvements in flexibility and in delayed-onset muscle soreness after sports massage.[22] A 2025 trial of 150 athletes described 40-minute deep tissue massage twice a week for 8 weeks and reported the greatest performance improvement in team and strength athletes.[23] Several studies found little or nothing. In the soreness trial, resting pain did not differ between the groups.[21] In 29 healthy volunteers, ten minutes of deep massage to the calf produced no change in calf muscle stiffness or ankle movement, and the authors concluded that using massage to increase tissue flexibility before activity is not justified.[24] In 9 people who did a hard cycling effort, deep massage, superficial massage and stretching did not change blood lactate levels compared with passive rest, and the authors concluded that the pressure used did not play a significant role.[25] In 19 competitive swimmers aged 12 to 20, deep massage and superficial (light-touch) massage between training sessions had no effect on sprint or functional performance, and the swimmers reported worse feelings of heaviness and pain at the main stages of swim training although they also reported less tiredness; the authors suggested the swimmers were able to train harder with no harm to recovery.[26] The 2020 review found no evidence that massage improved strength, jumping, sprinting, endurance or fatigue.[22] A 2016 review of 22 trials concluded that the effects of massage on performance recovery are rather small and partly unclear, and its authors questioned whether the limited effects justify using massage as a recovery method in competitive athletes.[27] In people with sore leg muscles after exercise, manual massage, real diathermy (a heating device) and sham diathermy produced no clinically relevant differences in pain scores right after the session, although scores on a patient-rated scale of global change did differ between the groups.[28] The 2025 athlete trial’s abstract describes no comparison group, and it measured outcomes with both objective and subjective assessments.[23] Where massage has been tested for short-term recovery after intense mixed training, the effects were medium in size: the 2016 review found medium positive effects after high-intensity mixed exercise, and shorter massage (5 to 12 minutes) tended to show larger effects than longer massage.[27] Relaxation and the Role of Pressure Several studies point to short-term relaxation after massage. A 2004 meta-analysis of 37 randomized studies found that a single massage was followed by lower state anxiety, blood pressure and heart rate.[29] In 263 volunteers with moderate or severe muscle spasm or strain who had a 45 to 60 minute deep tissue massage, average heart rate was 10.8 beats per minute lower and diastolic blood pressure 5.3 mm Hg lower afterward.[30] In 20 healthy adults, a reflex response in the calf muscle was weaker during massage than at rest, and weaker still during deep massage than during light massage; the study measured a laboratory reflex, not pain or movement.[31] In 60 healthy women, the two massage groups showed higher heart-rate variability than a resting group.[32] The picture is mixed, though. The same 2004 meta-analysis found no lower negative mood, cortisol or less immediate pain after a single massage.[29] In the 263-volunteer study, the lower systolic and mean arterial pressure did not clearly reach statistical significance, the abstract describes no comparison group, and its authors said additional research is warranted.[30] In the 60 healthy women, relaxation rose and stress fell in the resting group too.[32] Courses of massage have the more encouraging results: the largest effects in the 2004 meta-analysis came after a course of sessions rather than a single one, on measures of anxiety and mood.[29] In a pilot study of 54 adults aged 60 and over, twice-weekly massage for four weeks was followed by better scores for well-being and perceived stress than guided relaxation.[33] Sources Each number above links to the source. SECTIONS {"slug":"chair-massage","width":390,"sections":[{"anchor":"ts-what-it-is","label":"What it is","text":"What Is Chair Massage?Chair massage is a short massage you receive sitting up, fully clothed, in a padded portable chair that supports your chest, arms and head as you lean forward. I work through your clothing without oil, mostly on the back, shoulders, neck, arms and hands. A session usually lasts 10 to 20 minutes. The chair folds up and fits in a quiet corner, which is why chair massage is what I bring to employee appreciation days and workplace events.Most research on chair massage comes from small studies in workplaces and hospitals, usually with 15-minute sessions. In 52 employees, a 15-minute chair massage at work was followed by lower blood pressure, although the study had no comparison group.[1] In 38 nurses offered a weekly 15-minute chair massage for 10 weeks, perceived-stress scores were lower at the end.[2] In a randomized trial of 60 women on oncology nursing teams, 15-minute chair massages twice a week for three weeks were followed by lower stress scores, and less interference from pain in daily life, than no massage.[3] Studies of office workers given short chair massages over a month report less neck and back discomfort,[4][5] and one found a higher tolerance for pressure on tender muscle points.[5] These studies are small and short. I summarize them, including the weaker results, in the research section below.Chair massage is hands-on work by a licensed massage therapist, adapted to you as you give feedback. It is not a mechanical massage chair, and studies of those devices are not included here. These are general findings, not medical advice or a promise of any result; the full summaries, including the weaker results, are in the research section below."},{"anchor":"ts-common-reasons","label":"Common reasons","text":"Common Reasons Clients Choose Chair MassagePeople often choose chair massage when hours at a desk, on the phone or on their feet leave the neck, shoulders and upper back tight, and they want attention to those areas without changing clothes or taking an hour away from work. Others like it as a pause in a busy day, or as a first massage, since you stay dressed and the session is short. Employers book it for appreciation days and events, where each person takes a short turn in the chair.Research on chair massage for desk work points the same way, with limits. In 50 office workers, half had eight 15-minute chair massages during work breaks over four weeks and half had none; the massage group reported less pain in the upper and lower spine and the right arm, with smaller improvements in the right shoulder and left forearm, and tolerated more pressure on the muscle points tested before it hurt, most of all in the trapezius and supraspinatus muscles, while changes in the control group were not statistically significant.[5] In 124 computer workers randomly split among four weeks of chair massage, relaxing-music sessions or no intervention, the massage group had higher pressure-pain thresholds in every neck muscle tested and a higher relaxation level measured from heart-rate variability; the music group improved on relaxation but its pain thresholds were unchanged, falling in one muscle, and changes in the no-intervention group were negligible.[6] In 19 women in administration and management who had chair massage twice a week for a month, neck and upper-back discomfort scores fell and the neck bent further to the side and backward, although all 19 received the massage, with no separate control group, and only 15 completed the study.[4]Before I begin, I ask about your preferences and anything I should know about your health. You can request lighter pressure, a different focus, or a pause at any time."},{"anchor":"ts-who-can-benefit","label":"Who can benefit","text":"Who Can Benefit From Chair Massage?Chair massage suits people who want focused attention on the back, neck and shoulders in a short session, and groups where many people will take a turn. You do not need to undress or to have had a massage before, and you can ask me to stay with one area or to work more lightly. If you have an ongoing health condition, a recent injury or surgery, or you are pregnant, tell me at the start. I will keep the work within the scope of massage, adapt it or leave parts out, and I will tell you if I think you should check with a doctor first. If the chair itself is not comfortable for you, say so: I can adjust it or work with you seated upright in an ordinary chair."},{"anchor":"ts-guide-questions","label":"Questions","text":"Questions About Chair Massage Do I Need to Undress for Chair Massage?No. You stay fully clothed, and I do not use oil. Light layers are easiest to work through; a thick coat or a bulky hood is better taken off. How Long Is a Chair Massage?At corporate and group events I plan about 10 to 15 minutes per person, depending on the schedule and how many people take part. The Corporate & Group Massage page explains how the time block is planned. The studies summarized below mostly used 15-minute sessions. What Is the Chair Like?It is a padded folding chair that you sit on facing forward, with your knees on supports, your chest against a cushion and your face in a cradle, so your back, neck and shoulders are easy to reach. I adjust it to your height. If kneeling or leaning forward is uncomfortable, I can work with you seated upright in an ordinary chair. Is Chair Massage the Same as a Mechanical Massage Chair?No. A massage chair is a machine with rollers. Chair massage is hands-on work by a licensed massage therapist in a portable chair, adapted to you as you give feedback. How Much Pressure Will You Use?Enough to reach the tight muscles, and no more than you want. Tell me what you like, and ask me to lighten up or press more firmly at any time; I will adjust. How Is Chair Massage Different From Your Other Sessions?Chair massage is seated, clothed and short, and it focuses on the back, shoulders, neck, arms and hands. Therapeutic massage and deep tissue massage take place on a table, last longer and can cover the whole body. Thai massage is done on a mat and adds assisted stretching. Each is described on its own page. Can I Have a Chair Massage If I’m Pregnant or Have a Health Condition?Often yes, with changes. Tell me before I start about any health conditions, medications, pregnancy, recent injury or surgery. I may adjust the work, leave an area out, or suggest you check with your clinician first. Will I Feel the Results Right Away?People respond differently to massage, so I can’t promise a particular result or timeline. I will ask how the session feels and adjust as I go. What Does the Host Need to Provide?A quiet corner with roughly six feet by six feet of floor space, somewhere for people to wait, and a way for them to sign up for a time. I bring the chair and everything else. The Corporate & Group Massage page lists what I plan with you before the event. Serious events are rare: I ask about your health, medications, pregnancy and recent injuries before each session, even a short one at an event, and you can ask for lighter pressure or a pause at any time. Stress, Anxiety and Blood Pressure Several workplace studies report less stress and lower blood pressure after chair massage. In 52 employees, systolic and diastolic blood pressure were lower after a 15-minute chair massage at work.[1] In a study from the Touch Research Institute in Miami, 26 adults had a 15-minute chair massage and 24 sat in the massage chair to relax, twice a week for five weeks; anxiety was lower after the massage sessions but not the control sessions, brain-wave recordings in the massage group showed a pattern the authors read as alertness, the massage group became faster and more accurate at arithmetic, and at five weeks job-stress scores were lower only in the massage group.[16] In 28 employees randomly assigned to weekly massage at work for four weeks or to no massage, strain and blood pressure fell during the four massage weeks in the massage group but not in the control group.[17] In 48 insurance brokers at one company, 16 had a series of massages seated in a massage chair, 16 had them lying on a table and 16 had none; both massage groups improved on every burnout and anxiety measure, and the authors concluded that the position did not matter.[18] In 59 young healthy adults, a 17-minute seated acupressure massage was followed by lower anxiety and higher self-confidence scores than sitting in the chair without massage, with a slightly lower heart rate and a rise in the hormone oxytocin.[19] The limits are real. The 52-employee study had no comparison group, so the lower blood pressure cannot be separated from the effect of sitting quietly for 15 minutes.[1] In the Miami study, salivary cortisol was lower after massage only on the first day, and depression scores fell in both groups.[16] The 28-employee trial was small, and its abstract gives no figures.[17] The seated-acupressure study found no link between cortisol levels and how people felt, and no change in CGRP or in the marker IL-6.[19] In 60 nurses randomly assigned to a weekly 15-minute back massage for five weeks or to nothing, anxiety scores fell in the massage group and rose in the control group, but urinary cortisol and blood pressure did not differ significantly between the groups.[20] In 365 on-site aromatherapy massages with music given to emergency nurses over two 12-week periods, anxiety measured before and after the sessions was lower afterward, but occupational stress scores did not change over the 12 weeks and sick leave did not differ.[21] In 50 cardiac catheterization laboratory staff randomly assigned to 5 or 10 weekly 30-minute massages, with 10 further staff as controls, no significant effects were found on fatigue, pain, relaxation, stress or tension, even though 90 percent of appointments were used.[22] What is encouraging is how consistently the short-term effect appears: in every study above that measured anxiety before and after sessions, it was lower afterward,[16][19][21] and where massage was compared with sitting quietly in the same chair, the massage group did better.[16][19] Studies with a course of sessions over several weeks more often found changes in stress or burnout scores than single sessions did.[16][17][18] Desk Work, Muscle Discomfort and Movement Several chair massage studies looked at the discomfort that comes with sitting at a computer. In 50 office workers, eight 15-minute chair massages over four weeks were followed by less pain in the upper and lower spine and the right arm and by higher pressure-pain thresholds at every muscle point tested, with the largest change in the shoulder muscles on the left side, while changes in the control group were not statistically significant.[5] In 124 computer workers randomly assigned to four weeks of chair massage, relaxing music or nothing, chair massage raised the pressure-pain threshold in all the neck muscles tested and the relaxation level measured from heart-rate variability from 31.9 to 41.6 percent; music raised relaxation but left pain thresholds unchanged, with the threshold in one shoulder muscle falling, and changes in the control group were negligible.[6] In 19 women in administration and management who had chair massage twice a week for a month, neck side-bending improved from 42.4 to 48.3 degrees, neck extension from 63.2 to 67.2 degrees, and discomfort scores for the neck and upper back fell.[4] In 44 music students, eight 15-minute sessions of chair massage or exercises over four weeks raised the pressure-pain threshold at the most sensitive points in the upper shoulder muscles by 25 to 34 percent, most visibly in the massage group and from the fourth session on.[23] In a crossover study of 17 healthy adults, muscle activity in the upper shoulder muscles fell by 19 percent after a short, moderate-pressure massage of the shoulders and neck, compared with 1 percent after sitting quietly.[24] In a study from Thailand of 30 female administrative employees, 30 minutes of traditional Thai massage in each of three styles was followed by less forearm fatigue on muscle recordings.[25] The limits: all 19 women in the Ljubljana study received the massage, only 15 completed it, and its authors’ claim that twice-weekly sessions beat a single session rests on comparing phases within the same small group.[4] The 17-adult study measured muscle activity, not pain, and in the Thai study shoulder strength was not significantly different after massage.[24][25] In 45 cardiac sonographers randomly assigned to weekly 30-minute chair massage, massage plus stretching, or nothing for 10 weeks, discomfort scores improved somewhat in both massage groups, and the authors called for larger trials.[26] An employer-funded program of 20-minute on-site massages for long-term care staff showed possible improvements in job satisfaction and an early reduction in pain severity, with the greatest benefit in people who already had symptoms, but no long-term effect was demonstrated.[27] None of the studies that give their length followed people for longer than ten weeks. Still, the two office-worker studies are among the better-designed chair massage studies, with randomized control groups and an objective measure of pain sensitivity,[5][6] and together with the music-student study they agree that four weeks of short sessions changed how much pressure tender neck and shoulder muscles could take.[5][6][23] In 29 nursing students who had both a firm and a very light seated massage, the firm one was rated better for energy, pain, stress and feeling physically tense, which is why I ask you about pressure rather than keeping it light by default.[28] Nurses, Hospital Staff and Caregivers Hospitals have studied chair massage for their own staff and for visiting families. In 38 nurses offered a weekly 15-minute chair massage during work for 10 weeks, 329 of 400 appointments were used, and at 10 weeks perceived-stress scores had fallen from 17.85 to 14.92 and anxiety scores from 49.45 to 40.95, with better scores on a self-assessment scale and a symptom scale.[2] In the randomized trial of 60 women on oncology nursing teams in São Paulo, 15-minute chair massages twice a week for three weeks were followed by lower stress scores than no massage, with an effect size (a Cohen’s d of 1.21) that counts as large, and less interference from pain in general activity, mood, work and sleep.[3] In 12 hospital staff, mostly nurses, who had up to eight 15-minute Swedish massages at work, pain and tension were significantly lower, and relaxation and mood better, after massage, measured before and after each session.[29] Evaluations of chair massage services for carers of inpatients at a cancer hospital in Manchester, England, reported better physical and emotional scores that were retained to the next day, better sleep, and feel-good scores that rose from 5 to 8 out of 10 on a transplant unit.[30][31] In a quality improvement project at an academic medical center in New Jersey, chair massage was among the brief on-site practices offered to nursing staff over 11 months, and its use rose over the period.[32] Most of these are pilot studies or service evaluations without a comparison group, so they cannot show how much of the change came from the massage itself: the 38-nurse study, the 12-staff study and the two Manchester evaluations all compared people’s scores before and after massage, with no separate control group described.[2][29][30][31] The 2021 network meta-analysis found that massage reduced occupational stress in health care workers but that yoga did more, and the 2019 systematic review of aromatherapy and massage in nurses found that most studies reported a benefit but judged them too few and at too high a risk of bias to prove the effect.[9][12] In the 11-month project, staff perceptions of self-care opportunities and of a restorative work environment did not change significantly, and staffing and scheduling limited who could take part.[32] In the cardiac catheterization laboratory study described above, weekly massages produced no statistically significant effects, although the authors’ feasibility test supported further research on fatigue, pain, relaxation and tension.[22] The randomized oncology-nursing trial is the strongest chair massage study I found, and it is encouraging: six 15-minute sessions over three weeks were enough to show a large effect-size difference in stress between the groups.[3] The uptake numbers say something on their own: 329 of 400 appointments used by the nurses, 90 percent of appointments used by the catheterization laboratory staff, and 227 chair massages given to carers over two years on one transplant unit.[2][22][31] Sources Each number above links to the source.
